title: Jonathan Creek Mississippian center
summary: In Marshall County, Jonathan Creek was a planned Mississippian town with mounds, a plaza and strong walls, lived in from about AD 1200 to 1300.
bodyMarkdown:
Jonathan Creek was a large Mississippian mound center in Marshall County. Archaeologists record it as site 15Ml4. According to the [Kentucky Archaeological Survey's page on Jonathan Creek](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Find-a-Site/Pages/Jonathan-Creek.aspx), Native people lived in this community from about A.D. 1200 to 1300. They built a planned town with mounds, a plaza and strong defensive walls.

## Digging before the lake

The site was studied because it was about to be flooded. Members of the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC), working through the University of Kentucky, began excavations in 1940, before the site was flooded. The [Kentucky Heritage Council's survey of the Mississippi period](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Learn-More/Documents/Mississippi%20Period%20Chapter%20The%20Archaeology%20of%20Kentucky%20An%20update%20Volume%202.pdf) says the University of Kentucky worked at five sites in the reservoir area under the WPA and CCC, including Jonathan Creek.

The work ended with World War II. The Survey's site page says the men were drafted after America's entry into the war in 1942. The Heritage Council chapter says the project ended abruptly with U.S. entry into the war in late 1941. The first report on any of this work did not appear until 1952.

## A planned town

The CCC crews excavated less than a quarter of the site. Even so, they investigated all or part of more than 70 houses. They also recorded several platform mounds and burial mounds around an open plaza, the classic layout of a Mississippian town.

A stockade with bastions enclosed the town on three sides. A bastion is a fortified spur in the wall that gave defenders a platform. The Survey says the stockades show a sequence of building, repair and dismantling. Their shifting position reflects either the community's growth or a southward shift of its center.

The builders of the last and outermost stockade, the Survey says, made "a show of power" with its height and length.

## Two kinds of houses

Residents built two kinds of rectangular houses. Most were single-set post houses, with posts driven into the ground. About one-tenth were wall-trench houses, with posts set in a trench that was then filled with earth.

In the lower Ohio and central Mississippi valleys, wall-trench houses became more popular after A.D. 1200. The Survey suggests the mix at Jonathan Creek may reflect differences between conservative households and younger ones who adopted the new style.

## Reading old records anew

For decades the site was assigned to an early "Jonathan Creek phase" of about A.D. 1000–1150. Archaeologist Schroeder reexamined the old field notes, maps and artifacts in the 2000s. Her radiocarbon dates fall roughly between A.D. 1170 and 1280. The Heritage Council chapter says this shows the town was occupied well into the 1200s, later than the phase that bears its name.

## Kentucky today

The site was excavated because it was about to be flooded, and the CCC field records, reexamined by Schroeder, remain the main source on the town. Other Mississippian sites in the region include the [Chambers Site](/stories/chambers-site-15ml109-marshall-county/) in Marshall County and [Wickliffe Mounds](/stories/wickliffe-mounds-mississippian-village-ballard-county/) in Ballard County.
